name: Streetwear drops

lead: A streetwear drop is a small, time-limited release of clothing or sneakers, usually promoted on social media. Buyers use drops to get pieces from brands such as Supreme and Stussy that carry style status.

Wikipedia credits Supreme with popularising the model of weekly small releases rather than one full seasonal line, and notes it has since spread to other fashion brands. Limited supply has fed a resale market.

paras: Fans follow brand announcements, release days and collaborations, and buy at retail or on resale. Streetwear is typically styled as oversized, logo or graphic clothing and sneakers.
Risks are financial: scarcity pricing, resale markups and impulse spending. Critics of hype culture say it prioritises resale gain and prestige over style.

angle.text: Drops give access to clothing that carries trend and brand status, which people use to shape a distinctive wardrobe.

lead: Streetwear drops are limited, timed product releases in which a brand puts out a small batch of clothing, accessories or sneakers, often announced on social media.[1] The model gives buyers access to scarce pieces that serve as style signals.

Wikipedia credits Supreme with the weekly-drop model, with releases every Thursday online and in stores, and notes that fashion brands copied streetwear's drops.[2][1] Streetwear itself grew from late-1970s and 1980s New York hip-hop and West Coast surf and skate culture; Stussy shifted to exclusive boutique sales to create scarcity.[1]
In looksmaxxing, drops are a style meta: a way to refresh a wardrobe with currently fashionable pieces, alongside the cost and competition that scarcity creates.

paras: Brands limit production to create artificial scarcity, which encouraged limited editions and resale markets.[1] Hypebeast culture, once a derogatory label for trend-chasers, is tied to logo-heavy clothing and sneaker resale.[1]

Supreme opened in April 1994 on Lafayette Street in Manhattan and releases small groups of products weekly rather than a full seasonal line.[2] A 2020 Supreme-Nabisco Oreo cookie retailing at about $3 was listed by resellers for over $91,000 within a week.[2]

timeline.event: Dapper Dan opens his Harlem customisation boutique.[1]
VF Corporation agrees to buy Supreme for $2.1 billion.[2]
